 How We Can End Energy Poverty in the United States
 Fully funding the Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program could end energy poverty and lower all customer bills.
 By Joe Daniel , Maria Castillo , David Valdes , and Hilary Griggs

 The Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP) has served as the largest source for energy assistance nationwide for nearly 50 years, providing bill assistance to income qualified households to support access to home heating and cooling. Even so, LIHEAP is consistently underfunded, preventing the program from fully addressing energy insecurity in the United States. Nationally, only 17% of eligible households received LIHEAP assistance in 2024.
 RMI analysis of electricity and gas bills nationwide found that a fully funded LIHEAP would not only significantly reduce low-income energy bills and energy burdens but could also provide an additional $17 billion in systemwide benefits lowering costs for all customers. Increasing annual LIHEAP assistance funding by $25 billion, less than 0.5% of the federal budget, could reduce annual low-income energy bills by $1,016. This bill reduction would mean that customers receiving assistance would, on average, spend no more than 6% of their income on energy bills (6% is the widely accepted benchmark for a high energy burden).
 Expanding and fully funding LIHEAP assistance would also help lower energy bills and rates for all customers, lowering average household gas and electric bills by a total of $252 annually and rates by an average of 4% due to revenue savings from avoided uncollectibles.
 Exhibit 1 
 Current LIHEAP funding provides $4 billion dollars of assistance annually, which is critical for helping income-qualified customers but insufficient for addressing the systemic problem of energy poverty. RMI calculated the LIHEAP funding needed to reduce household energy burdens to a maximum of 6%. The results found that funding would need to increase to $31 billion to serve 100% of eligible households to the level of a combined 6% energy burden for home gas and electricity costs. This total includes $29 billion in energy assistance and a $1.7 billion increase in administrative funding.
 Exhibit 2 
 While LIHEAP provides essential assistance for income-qualified families, the program also benefits all ratepayers. The largest benefit is from avoided “arrears,” the debt associated with customers that fall behind on their utility bills. Nationwide, total household arrears could reach $25 billion by the end of 2026 . Utilities are allowed to recover the costs of these unpaid bills (sometimes called “uncollectibles”) by charging all customers. The assistance provided by LIHEAP supports customers to better pay their bills, in turn lowering arrears and as a result lowering costs for all customers.
 Reducing arrears also helps utilities with their cash flow, reduces carrying costs, and provides widespread benefits to the utility in the form of reduced costs associated with disconnections, bill management plans, reduced customer calls, and other costs, all of which are ultimately put on ratepayers. RMI conservatively estimates that this adds up to $17 billion in benefits to all ratepayers (residential, commercial, and industrial).

 Methodology
 In order to calculate what a fully funded LIHEAP would look like, RMI calculated (1) the amount of energy assistance that would be required to get all LIHEAP eligible households down to a 6% energy burden — home electric and gas combined — and (2) the increased administrative costs that would be needed to increase participation from 16% of eligible households to 100%.
 The rate and bill impacts reflect simplified assumptions around average rates and bills and do not account for rate design and structure, which vary across the country by jurisdiction. The average bill reduction for residential households includes both LIHEAP participants and non-participants. The amount of required energy assistance was calculated at the state level based on the amount of assistance required to reduce the average energy burden in each income group to 6%.
 In order to see the benefit from increased LIHEAP funding and participation at this scale, changes to its structure and administration will be necessary. For example, current state allocation for funding favors states with larger winter heating demands and does not adequately address summer cooling needs in warm-weather states. However, our analysis assumes allocation is designed to meet energy burden demands regardless of whether the need is for cooling or heating. The costs associated with these changes would be covered by the near 6x increase in administrative costs that we included in the cost calculation (from $338 million to $2 billion — totaling only 7% of the total funding increase).
 Our findings on the benefits of this increased funding for ratepayers are based on analysis from RMI’s Energy Poverty Policy Simulator (EPPS), which calculates the reduced arrears linearly with reduced energy burden. Results from EPPS are consistent with various utility findings , which also show additional ratepayer benefits from reducing energy burden such as reduced carrying costs, reduced costs associated with disconnections, and other benefits. Our approach to calculating these benefits was conservative compared to many utility filings, some of which reported nearly twice what we assumed. We also omitted benefit streams like reduced administrative costs associated with customer calls . As a result, the ratepayer benefits of a fully funded LIHEAP may be more extensive than our analysis shows.
